old_entry.title: Crazy Taxi
old_entry.summary: Crazy Taxi is a racing video game developed and published by Sega.
body: Crazy Taxi is a racing video game developed and published by Sega. It is the first game in the Crazy Taxi series. In the game, players are tasked with picking up taxi customers and driving to their destination as quickly as possible. It was first released in arcades in 1999 then ported to other consoles starting with the Sega Dreamcast in 2000.

The game received generally positive reviews across most versions, with the Dreamcast port garnering critical acclaim. Critics praised its difficulty curve and the gameplay as "addictive". Reception to the implementation of the soundtrack was more mixed. In retrospect, Crazy Taxi has been regarded as one of the greatest video games of all time. It became one of the few Sega All Stars on the Dreamcast and earned Greatest Hits and Player's Choice status on PlayStation 2 and GameCube respectively. The game has been rereleased numerous times, and was featured on the Dreamcast Collection in 2011. The core gameplay of Crazy Taxi has inspired other games and numerous clones. The game's success on consoles prompted Sega to continue the series, starting with Crazy Taxi 2 in 2001.

old_entry.title: Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver
old_entry.subtitle: Soul Reaver Uses Two Versions of One World to Tell a Revenge Story
old_entry.summary: On August 16, 1999 Soul Reaver moved Legacy of Kain from a top-down perspective into a three-dimensional adventure centered on Raziel.
body: On August 16, 1999 Soul Reaver moved Legacy of Kain from a top-down perspective into a three-dimensional adventure centered on Raziel. Betrayed by Kain and transformed into a wraith, the protagonist crosses Nosgoth by reading the same space in material and spectral states. Personal revenge therefore becomes a navigation rule: identity, architecture and abilities change together. Crystal Dynamics builds a gothic world where story is not separate from exploration, because Raziel's condition literally determines which routes exist.

The player controls Raziel, a disfigured and ghostly vampire. The game is normally shown from a third-person perspective behind Raziel, but players can rotate the viewpoint around him. Gameplay relies largely on shifting between the material and spectral planes of existence to progress through areas. Although interaction with objects is limited in the spectral realm, this can be advantageous, because Raziel can phase through otherwise impassable gates there, and water is insubstantial, allowing him to walk on lakebeds; however, blocks, doors, and switches can be manipulated only in the physical realm. Many puzzles are based on the differences between the two realms; for example, platforms and environment features in one realm may change form to open new paths in the other. Block puzzles are also common and require the rotation, flipping, and moving of large blocks to progress, often with a time limit and while avoiding enemies.

At first, Raziel can jump, glide using his torn wings, move blocks, and pick up and throw objects and enemies. Initially unarmed, he fights using his claws, but can alternatively use weapons such as rocks, torches, spears and staffs, and the Soul Reaver. Raziel can freely shift to the spectral realm, but can return to the material realm only through special portals when at full health. Raziel automatically shifts to the spectral realm if he runs out of health. As the game progresses, Raziel gains the powers of his clan brothers after defeating them and becomes able to phase through gates in the spectral realm and climb walls in the material realm. Initially vulnerable to water, he overcomes this weakness and learns to swim.

The protagonist of Soul Reaver is the vampire-turned-wraith Raziel, whom Kain casts to death at the beginning of the game. Although Kain is the protagonist of the previous game, Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain, he is the primary antagonist and final boss of Soul Reaver. The Elder God resurrects and assists Raziel, explains the game's controls, and describes previous events in the story. Ariel, who preceded Kain as the guardian of the Pillar of Balance, appears as a spirit and offers Raziel advice on occasion. During his quest, Raziel meets his brothers - Melchiah, Zephon, Rahab and Dumah - who serve as the game's bosses. Each has developed different powers that Raziel partially gains by killing them and devouring their souls. A fifth brother, Turel, was omitted due to time constraints on development.

old_entry.summary: Tekken Tag Tournament is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by Namco for arcades.
body: Tekken Tag Tournament is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It is a spin-off the Tekken series. Not canon to the main storyline, Tekken Tag Tournament features nearly all the characters in the previous Tekken games and introduces a two-on-two 'tag team' battle mechanic. It was released as an arcade game, before becoming a North American and European launch title for the PlayStation 2 in 2000. The arcade version ran on the same Namco System 12 board with a 32-bit engine as Tekken 3, while the ported home console version received upgraded graphics.

A follow-up, Tekken Tag Tournament 2, was released in 2011. A remastered version of the game titled Tekken Tag Tournament HD was released for the PlayStation 3 in November 2011, as part of Tekken Hybrid.

old_entry.title: Final Fantasy VIII
old_entry.subtitle: Junction, Memory and Adolescence
old_entry.summary: Final Fantasy VIII begins with young people training for a profession that sends them into a war.
body: Final Fantasy VIII begins with young people training for a profession that sends them into a war. Squall belongs to Balamb Garden, a school for mercenaries, and becomes a member of SeeD. Released for PlayStation in Japan in 1999, the game moves between school life, military assignments and his growing relationship with Rinoa.

Guardian Forces do more than appear as summoned creatures. Junctioning them opens abilities and lets stored magic improve a character's statistics. Draw supplies spells from enemies and other sources. Because a spell can be both something to cast and something to keep equipped, the inventory becomes part of character building.

Triple Triad places a compact card game inside this much larger journey. Its cards can be collected and played against people encountered along the way. Alongside the main battles and scenes, it gives towns and schools another reason to be revisited: someone there may have a hand worth challenging.

old_entry.title: Super Smash Bros.
old_entry.subtitle: The Fighting Game That Turned the Crossover into a Rule
old_entry.summary: Nintendo released Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 64 in Japan on January 21, 1999.
body: Nintendo released Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 64 in Japan on January 21, 1999. Behind the meeting of Mario, Link, Pikachu and Kirby, however, was a far more abstract prototype: Dragon King: The Fighting Game, developed by Masahiro Sakurai with Satoru Iwata handling programming. The breakthrough was not simply adding famous characters. Smash changed the problem of the fighting game: instead of emptying a life bar, players accumulate damage so that opponents become progressively easier to launch out of the stage. Four players, items, platforms and readable rules turn combat into controlled chaos. The crossover works because every Nintendo icon is translated into movement, weight, attacks and space rather than displayed merely as a reference.

The first Super Smash Bros. began without Nintendo characters. In the prototype called Dragon King: The Fighting Game, Masahiro Sakurai handled planning, specifications, graphics, modelling and movement while Satoru Iwata programmed almost the entire project himself during weekends. The goal was already clear: find an alternative to the dominant two-dimensional fighting games and build a four-player battle around the Nintendo 64 analogue stick. Four anonymous figures forced the prototype to prove the value of its rules before it could rely on the strength of famous brands. Mario, Link and the others arrived only later. That order matters: Smash was not born as a museum of mascots, but as a combat experiment that discovered Nintendo characters were the perfect language for making its ideas immediately understandable.

Smash changes a fundamental fighting-game convention. Hits do not directly empty a life bar until defeat; they raise a percentage that makes the character easier to launch farther away. The real threat is therefore the edge of the stage. Health and position become one system: taking damage means losing spatial stability, while survival depends on trajectory, jumping and the ability to return to the platform. The rule is easy to explain even to players who do not know long combinations, yet it produces sophisticated decisions. A weak attack can reposition, a strong one can finish an exchange, and the same move changes value depending on percentage and distance from the boundary. Combat becomes a continuous negotiation with space rather than only with an opponent's body.

Sakurai wanted a four-player battle royale, and Nintendo 64 provided four controller ports without adapters. Putting four fighters on the same screen, however, creates a readability problem: the camera must contain them, stages need both space and danger, and items must alter the rhythm without erasing the ability to understand what happened. Smash responds with strong silhouettes, immediate directional attacks and arenas built around recognizable platforms. Items introduce temporary disruptions, while handicaps and teams let groups adjust differences in skill. The game does not remove chaos; it frames it. A match remains noisy and unpredictable, but readable enough to generate instant stories: who launched whom, which item reversed the fight, and who managed to return from the edge.

old_entry.title: Ape Escape
old_entry.summary: Ape Escape is a 1999 platform game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
body: Ape Escape is a 1999 platform game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. The first game in the Ape Escape series, the game tells the story of an ape named Specter who gains enhanced intelligence and a malevolent streak through the use of an experimental helmet. Specter produces an army of apes, which he sends through time in an attempt to rewrite history. Spike, the player character, sets out to capture the apes with the aid of special gadgets.

Ape Escape is played from a third-person perspective. Players use a variety of gadgets to pursue and capture the apes, traversing across several environments. The game's controls are heavily centered around the analog sticks, being the first game to require the use of the PlayStation's DualShock controller. Development of Ape Escape lasted over two years, and was generally focused on adapting to the use of the controller, which was a significant challenge for the development team.

Ape Escape was met with critical acclaim from critics, with praise particularly directed at the innovative use of the dual analog controls, as well as the graphics and music; the voice acting received minor criticism. The game is widely considered to be one of the greatest on the PlayStation console, and received several re-releases. The game also spawned numerous sequels and spin-offs, beginning with Ape Escape 2 in 2002. A remake, Ape Escape P, was released for the PlayStation Portable in 2005 to mixed reviews.

old_entry.title: System Shock 2
old_entry.subtitle: System Shock 2 Makes Fear a Consequence of Systems
old_entry.summary: On August 11, 1999 System Shock 2 was released for Windows in the United States.
body: On August 11, 1999 System Shock 2 was released for Windows in the United States. Irrational Games and Looking Glass combined first-person shooting, role-playing statistics, scarce resources, hacking and environmental storytelling. Horror does not depend only on monsters; it comes from making decisions when ammunition, abilities and information are insufficient. Audio logs let the Von Braun narrate its collapse without constantly interrupting exploration, while SHODAN remains a presence capable of turning interface and voice into instruments of threat.

As in its predecessor, System Shock, gameplay in System Shock 2 is an amalgamation of the action role-playing game and survival horror genres. The developers achieved this gameplay design by rendering the experience as a standard first-person shooter and adding a character customization and development system, which are considered signature role-playing elements. The player uses melee and projectile weapons to defeat enemies, while the role-playing system allows the development of useful abilities. Navigation is presented from a first-person view and complemented with a heads-up display that shows character and weapon information, a map, and a drag and drop inventory.

The backstory is explained progressively through the player's acquisition of audio logs and encounters with ghostly apparitions. At the beginning of the game, the player chooses a career in a branch of the Unified National Nominate, a fictional military organization. Each branch of service gives the player a set of starting bonuses composed of certain skills, though may thereafter freely develop as the player chooses. The Marine begins with bonuses to weaponry, the Navy officer is skilled in repairing and hacking, and the OSA agent gets a starting set of psionic powers.

Development of System Shock 2 began in 1997 when Looking Glass Studios approached Irrational Games with an idea to co-develop a game. The development team were fans of System Shock and sought to create a similar game. Early story ideas were similar to the novella Heart of Darkness. In an early draft, the player was tasked with assassinating an insane commander on a starship. The original title, according to its pitch document, was Junction Point. The philosophy of the design was to continue to develop the concept of a dungeon crawler, like Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss, in a science fiction setting, the basis for System Shock. However, the press mistook System Shock to be closer to a Doom clone which was cited for its poor financial success. With Junction Point, the goal was to add in significant role-playing elements and a persistent storyline as to distance the game from Doom.

old_entry.title: Dance Dance Revolution Solo Bass Mix
old_entry.subtitle: DDR Solo Bass Mix Redesigns the Dance Pad Around a Single Body
old_entry.summary: On August 19, 1999 Konami released Dance Dance Revolution Solo Bass Mix in Japanese arcades.
body: On August 19, 1999 Konami released Dance Dance Revolution Solo Bass Mix in Japanese arcades. Its dance platform adds diagonal directions and offers three- or six-panel configurations, shifting body weight differently from the familiar four-arrow layout. A soundtrack tied to Dancemania BASS also gives the game a personality distinct from the main series. It is a concrete example of how a peripheral can change choreography, difficulty and posture: the software does not merely ask players to read more symbols, but to reconsider where the body itself must move.

Gameplay in the Solo series is nearly identical to that of the main Dance Dance Revolution series, but with a few differences to optimize the game for single-player mode.  In addition to the four-panel mode offered in the main series, Solo adds a three-panel mode in its Bass Mix and 2000 releases, as well as a six-panel mode in all of its releases.  Both modes add two new panels: up-left and up-right.  The three-panel mode adds the down arrow to these, while the six-panel mode combines both the four traditional panels and the two new panels.

It was released as an arcade game by Konami on August 19, 1999 in Japan. The game premiered 16 songs to the series and takes its name, as well as most of its soundtrack, from the Dancemania BASS albums. This is the first game that features a live-action intro.

Dance Dance Revolution Solo is a series of games spun off of the main Dance Dance Revolution series. It consists of three arcade releases in Japan. The game mode was also adapted for use in a children's arcade version and two console releases (as a game mode).

original.old_heading: System 573 connects physical movement to arcade technology
original.old_body: Under the platform sits Konami's System 573 hardware, handling graphics, audio and cabinet input. DDR demonstrates that an arcade rhythm game is not software alone: sensors, panels and display together form the instrument on which the performance is played. Sound does not merely accompany action: it organizes anticipation, energy and recognition. Timbre, rhythm and repetition give decisions a temporal structure and can make a rule memorable before the image does. The result remains recognizable because form and function move together, without separating the idea from the way it is experienced.

old_entry.title: Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage!
old_entry.summary: Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage!, known as Spyro 2: Gateway to Glimmer in PAL regions, is a 1999 platform game developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.
body: Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage!, known as Spyro 2: Gateway to Glimmer in PAL regions, is a 1999 platform game developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. It is the second installment in the Spyro series and a sequel to Spyro the Dragon (1998).

The game begins with Spyro planning to take a vacation after his previous adventures. However, he is unexpectedly transported to the realm of Avalar, where the malevolent sorcerer Ripto has emerged and is wreaking havoc. Spyro joins forces with the inhabitants of Avalar to confront Ripto and put an end to his destructive reign.

Ripto’s Rage! introduced several new mechanics not present in its predecessor, such as swimming, climbing, and power-up gates that temporarily grant Spyro abilities like superflame or flight. Levels also feature side quests, mini-games, and boss battles, adding more variety and complexity than the first game.

The game received positive reviews from critics, who praised its colorful graphics, improved gameplay variety, and larger amount of content. It was followed by Spyro: Year of the Dragon in 2000, and later remade as part of the Spyro Reignited Trilogy in 2018.

old_entry.title: Homeworld
old_entry.subtitle: A Fleet Carries Its Home With It
old_entry.summary: A real-time strategy game set in three-dimensional space, where ships and losses carry across a journey into exile.
body: Homeworld brings real-time strategy into truly three-dimensional space, forcing players to think above and below the usual plane of the map. But its identity also grows from the continuity of the fleet: ships, losses and resources carry across missions and turn the campaign into a material journey. The mothership, the story of exile and a soundtrack designed to suggest distance and solemnity make space warfare a story of collective survival rather than military expansion alone.

Homeworld asks players to consider positions above and below a target, not only around it. This freedom requires an interface capable of making distances understandable when a flat map is no longer sufficient. The player must build a three-dimensional representation of the battlefield and alternate between an overall view and local attention. The novelty therefore does not lie only in showing ships that fly. It concerns the kind of problem that has to be solved. An approach can exploit a less obvious direction, while a formation has to be read through the volume it occupies. Strategy becomes an exercise in spatial orientation, in which seeing well is part of the ability to command. The interface does not remove complexity, but tries to turn it into something that can be manipulated.

The mothership concentrates production functions and narrative meaning, becoming the reference point around which the fleet is organized. It is not simply a base that can be rebuilt elsewhere if the situation changes. Its presence gives continuity to the journey and makes defense a central responsibility. The player has to project force without forgetting what makes it possible to continue. This tension links expansion to protection. Sending units far away can open opportunities, but also creates distances that must be crossed if a threat reaches the center. The ship's form thus becomes recognizable through its function. It represents home not only because the story says so, but because the system organizes the very possibility of a future around its survival.

The persistence of units through the campaign links one battle to the next. Saving a ship can matter beyond the immediate victory, and a loss does not disappear completely when the scenario changes. This relationship makes efficiency important, but also attention to what is preserved. The player does not manage only an abstract army generated for a single challenge. They accompany a group that accumulates a history through its changing state. Continuity can create difficulty if the next mission begins with too little preparation, but that is precisely what gives choices weight. Winning by spending everything and winning while preserving a margin are not equivalent outcomes. The journey asks the player to think of the current battle as part of a longer responsibility.

old_entry.title: Valkyrie Profile
old_entry.subtitle: Listening to a life before recruiting it
old_entry.summary: On December 22, 1999, tri-Ace released Valkyrie Profile for PlayStation in Japan.
body: On December 22, 1999, tri-Ace released Valkyrie Profile for PlayStation in Japan. The player takes the role of Lenneth, a Valkyrie charged by Odin with finding the souls of fallen warriors, the Einherjar, and preparing them for the divine war of Ragnarok. This premise changes the normal structure of a role-playing game: many characters are first encountered through the final moments of their lives before joining the party, and the available time is organized into periods that force the player to choose where to go and whom to develop. Combat assigns each party member to a controller button, turning the coordination of attacks into combos and special moves. Choices and actions also lead to different endings. Valkyrie Profile thus combines Norse mythology, time management and rhythmic action to build an RPG in which recruiting someone means first listening to their loss.

tri-Ace describes Valkyrie Profile as the story of a Valkyrie who descends to Midgard to gather the souls of warriors worthy of fighting in Ragnarok. The narrative consequence is radical: many future party members are introduced as their lives are about to end. Before evaluating statistics or usefulness, the player witnesses relationships, failures, desires and circumstances that lead them to death. Recruitment therefore carries a different weight from an ordinary tavern encounter. Every Einherjar brings a completed story and, at the same time, a second function within Lenneth's party. The game thus builds an archive of brief lives converging in the conflict of the gods. The variety of characters does not simply broaden battle combinations, but shows how many forms human fragility can take.

Valkyrie Profile's combat assigns the active party members to the controller's face buttons. Pressing a button calls that character's attack, and the order in which they are combined determines the height, timing and continuity of a combo. Official descriptions of later releases still identify combos and special attacks as foundational features of the system. The player therefore does not simply select a technique from a menu, but builds a sequence by observing how strikes interact. Launching an enemy, keeping it airborne and chaining attacks becomes a form of temporal composition. Each character adds a different rhythm, and an effective party does not depend only on numerical values. The controller itself becomes a small keyboard: four buttons, four bodies, a series of inputs that must arrive at the right moment to become damage and spectacle.

Modern versions of Valkyrie Profile continue to explicitly present multiple endings determined by actions and choices. In the original, this structure speaks directly to Lenneth's role: the protagonist initially serves as an instrument of the gods, but the player can pay attention to relationships, memories and signs that call that function into question. Progress therefore does not consist only of preparing effective warriors for Asgard. There is a second reading of the journey, less obvious, that requires curiosity and a different use of the available time. The ending system turns interpretation into a practice. Simply following orders produces a coherent story; looking for further connections can open another. It is a particularly fitting choice for a game about memory and destiny, because it suggests that understanding one's identity depends not only on what is told, but on what one decides to observe.

old_entry.title: Shenmue
old_entry.subtitle: Life goes on even while you wait
old_entry.summary: On December 29, 1999, SEGA released Shenmue: Chapter 1 Yokosuka for Dreamcast in Japan.
body: On December 29, 1999, SEGA released Shenmue: Chapter 1 Yokosuka for Dreamcast in Japan. Yu Suzuki developed the project from an idea born on Sega Saturn and transformed it into a three-dimensional world where investigation unfolds within everyday time. Residents have routines, shops open and close, the sky changes, the clock advances and some information is available only at certain hours. SEGA describes Time Control and Magic Weather as central systems for creating a second reality, alongside motion capture, full voice acting and characters with behaviors of their own. Combat, training, arcades, collectibles and Quick Time Events are added to this foundation. Shenmue did not single-handedly invent the modern open world, but it demonstrates how the simulation of ordinary life can become narrative structure rather than mere decoration.

In Shenmue, the passage of time is a rule that organizes the investigation. SEGA cites Time Control among the systems used to build a realistic world, and the consequence is immediate: people and activities do not remain motionless waiting for the protagonist. A shop may be closed, a character may be elsewhere, and an appointment may require arriving at the right hour. This forces the player to live with intervals that other games might have removed. Waiting is not always spectacular, but it makes Yokosuka believable as a place with a rhythm independent of Ryo. Even a failed search becomes temporal information: returning later may produce a different situation. Shenmue thus turns the clock from an indicator into narrative structure, because the sequence of events also depends on when the player chooses to look for them.

SEGA emphasizes that Shenmue's characters are fully voiced and have life patterns of their own. This production choice is enormous because many residents do not exist merely as containers for one useful line. They move, work, return home and can be encountered in different places depending on the time. For the player, this means learning the city through its people as well. Asking for information becomes a form of social navigation: knowing who frequents a district or who might know something helps narrow the search. The system does not produce a perfect simulation and many routines are necessarily limited, but it changes the tone of the investigation. Yokosuka feels less like a series of hotspots and more like a collection of lives that Ryo temporarily interrupts with his questions. Credibility comes from the continuity between what a character says and the place where they are encountered.

Magic Weather allows Shenmue to change atmospheric conditions as its internal calendar advances. SEGA presents the system alongside Time Control as part of building a believable alternative reality. Rain, snow or a different sky do more than change the image. They alter the memory of a street the player crosses dozens of times and make the passage of days visible during the investigation. The same Dobuita can feel more welcoming or more hostile without changing geometry. This use of variation is particularly effective in a game that asks players to return often to the same places. Instead of constantly seeking new areas, Shenmue invests in the temporal transformation of existing ones. Weather thus becomes an economical and narratively coherent way to prevent everyday repetition from feeling completely static.

Shenmue popularizes the term Quick Time Event for sequences in which the player must respond rapidly to contextual prompts while the camera maintains tightly controlled direction. SEGA's page for the re-releases remembers the game as one of the pioneers of this form, while industry literature connects the QTE name to Yu Suzuki. The function is clear: enable chases, dodges and spectacular actions without requiring a complete system for every gesture shown. The advantage is strong cinematic continuity; the risk is reducing a complex situation to a binary response. In Shenmue, QTEs nevertheless become part of a broader vocabulary, alternating with slow exploration and free combat. It is precisely the contrast that makes the sudden change of rhythm memorable when an everyday scene turns into a test of reaction.

SEGA explicitly remembers arcades and minigames among the elements capable of absorbing the player beyond the main story. In Shenmue this detour is significant because Ryo is searching for his father's killer, yet the world continues to offer capsule toys, training, video games and small everyday activities. The game does not erase narrative tension; it accepts that a person can waste time even during a dramatic period. Entering an arcade and starting a SEGA machine also places arcade culture inside the reconstruction of the city. The detour becomes part of the place's credibility and of the history of the company that produced it. Shenmue therefore uses free time as world-building material. The player decides when to suspend the investigation and, precisely because of that freedom, the city seems to contain more possibilities than those strictly necessary to solve it.

Yu Suzuki's Game Developers Conference postmortem reconstructs Shenmue as a project initially born around Virtua Fighter and developed for Sega Saturn before migrating to Dreamcast. The platform change is not a simple technical upgrade. It allows greater character density, movement quality, three-dimensional environments and the amount of data required by a city that must react to time. SEGA also connects Shenmue to the technological evolution developed through Virtua Fighter and to the Dreamcast's ability to support a project of unusual scale for the period. This production history helps explain the finished game: many of its peculiarities come from the ambition to simulate aspects that established genres tended to simplify. Shenmue does not emerge from an already stable formula, but from years of attempts to turn an idea of interactive everyday life into executable software.
